title: EU watchdog says smart glasses must give 'clear warnings' when recording
key_facts: The European Data Protection Board (EDPB), the EU's central data regulator, said on Tuesday (13 Oct 2026) that smart glasses should give 'clear warnings' when recording, after a public outcry in recent months over secretly filmed footage of girls and women.
The guidance to users and manufacturers is non-binding; the EDPB says smart glasses raise 'serious privacy concerns'.
EDPB chair Anu Talus said the glasses 'look like ordinary glasses' but have cameras and microphones and are online, so people may be recorded without their knowledge.

Suggested warnings include bright LED lights, audio signals or voice activation cues, privacy-friendly smartphone notifications, or unique designs; they must be 'reliable, hard to ignore, and always up to date'.
The EDPB warned of greater risks in sensitive spaces such as schools and hospitals and public spots such as beaches, and for children.
People who share glasses footage on public social media or in official or professional activities must follow EU data protection rules.

Meta's glasses, made with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, are the most popular worldwide with sales in the millions and a blinking LED when recording; Google and Snap are preparing their own AI glasses.

Norway's government said last week it wants a temporary ban on smart glasses in certain public places; Oslo already bans camera glasses in schools; a 'Stop Smart Glasses' petition in Britain and Ireland passed 10,000 signatures, so the UK government must respond.
quote_evidence: The European Union's central data regulator on Tuesday said smart glasses should give "clear warnings" when they are recording, after a public outcry in recent months over secretly filmed footage of girls and women.
These warnings need to be reliable, hard to ignore, and always up to date.
why_it_matters_hint: Europe's top privacy regulator wants camera glasses to make recording obvious to the people around the wearer.
